summary:
This L0009 run was started by the line's timer, not by an instruction. It had no 'Asked' items, so the empty answers list is right. It made no claims. It built stage four, moving stacks fed back into the event loop (branch method/rest, c6dfd4d). It registered and ran one experiment, E0104 (the three 2D stall layers), and recorded it as falsified. The verdict stands: no layer completed a cycle. But part of what the summary and the line's state say about the other two layers is wrong.

What reproduces. In a fresh clone of c6dfd4d, the session's own script (feed_capped.py, seed 1, f* 0.3) gave the same stack counts and engine counters as evidence/E0104-results.json, bit for bit: 28 stacks built, 7 joins, 28 breaks, 38 spans, 661 integrator pieces, 505 contact searches, 10645 events. It stopped on the same 'rider and free sphere overlap'. Python time in stacks was 54.3 s against 54.1 s recorded. The recorded files in A0198 match their SHA-256. The new code path plainly acted.

What is wrong.
(1) The other two layers did not 'make no progress'. Their logs are empty because feed_capped.py prints nothing until it finishes, not because no step completed. I reran the same code with a print after every 0.01 step. Seed 2 at f* 0.3, whose old first stack event was at 5.823, ran to 6.24, building 27 stacks and breaking 22. Seed 1 at f* 0.4, old event at 4.910, ran to 5.25, building 19 stacks and breaking 17. Each then stuck inside one step for more than four minutes. So all three stall layers pass their old stall times with stacks fed back, two of them by 0.3 to 0.4 time units. The headline ('one 2D stall layer gets past its old stall time for the first time'), the E0104 outcome, and the evidence ('the first 0.01 step containing stack work did not finish') say otherwise. The line's state sentence 'The two neighbouring stall layers made no reported progress in about 705 s of CPU each' is literally true but misleading, and needs replacing.
(2) Where the CPU goes is now known, at least at f* 0.4. I logged every stack handler call in the step after 5.25. Time stops advancing at t = 5.252841380439. From there the loop repeats one cycle without end. A slow touch on a rider builds a stack (about 2.9 s of Python). A touch on it joins a third sphere and starts a new stack (about 4.6 s). A second touch breaks it (0.01 s). Then the same build happens again at the same instant. In about five minutes it went round over 35 times. This is a same-instant loop of the kind D0087's break-then-collide rule was meant to stop, now running through join and rebuild. It is not integrator cost. I did not trace seed 2.
(3) The seed 1 layer reached 5.89, not 5.88. t_reached is set only when a step completes, and the evidence records it as 5.89. The overlap error is in the step to 5.90. The summary, outcome and line state say 'reaches 5.88' and 'the step to 5.89'.
(4) The line note says 'about a second of Python per stack'. The summary says about two. The evidence gives 54.1 s over 28 stacks, 1.9 s each, so the note is wrong.

Numbers the summary uses that are not in the evidence. 'Hit at about twice the rest speed' and 'a stack lasts about a thousandth of a time unit' appear in no evidence file. I measured both in the seed 1 run, which was not perturbed by the measuring: its counts match. Of 34 touches on stack spheres, 26 came faster than the rest speed (0.01) and broke the stack. Their median approach speed was 0.017. 25 of the 26 were below the wake speed (0.05), and only one, at 0.072, was above it. Stacks that broke lived a median 0.0005 time units, at most 0.0023. Four were broken at the instant they were made. So 'about twice the rest speed' is a little high: 1.7 times is the median. 'About a thousandth' is the right order. These numbers support the question to Chris: under the immovable-bounce rule, 25 of the 26 breaks in this stretch would have been bounces.

One point about that question's framing. It says the immovable bounce 'adds a new place where a sphere is treated as infinitely heavy'. The join rule already in D0087 does this. On a slow touch, the stack sphere's velocity is left unchanged, the touching sphere takes the whole change, and the difference is booked as plate work. It does this even when the touched sphere is the top of a stack, not on the plate. Horizontal momentum is not audited, so that change goes unrecorded. It is small (below the rest speed), but Chris should know that both options treat the stack as immovable at a touch.

Energy. The session said nothing about energy could be judged. The books can be checked at every completed step. I synchronized copies of all spheres, so riders' pending plate work is booked, and computed the layer energy change minus plate work and the three losses. In seed 1 it stays at or below 3.4e-13 through the whole stack stretch to 5.89. The engine's gain counter is zero, and the largest plate snap at a hand-back is 3.2e-6. This shows the books close. It is not an audit over a completed cycle.

Housekeeping. program check passes apart from my own scratch, which I removed. The latest approval is approved/20261124T031934, more than a day old. The data folder is 736 megabytes of 15 gigabytes, with 82 gigabytes free against a floor of 40. tmp/ is empty and active.jsonl is empty. I found nothing written outside the program's folders in the run's window, and no new pytest folders under ~/.tmp, so last review's pytest-scratch point has not recurred. The summary's budget line (562.2 CPU-hours spent this week) is stale. program check gives 290.5 for the week, and L0018's summary the same night gave 293.6. 562.2 is the previous figure plus this run's 0.8.

My previous review raised one point: '125 or more integrator steps' cited without evidence. The question it was in was not asked again, so it lapses. My caveat that offline durations are not stack lifetimes in a layer is borne out by this run, and the session says so.

run_conditions.assessment: The run started at 05:05:17 UTC, 17 seconds after its scheduled time. It ended at 05:53:07, which matches its final commit at 05:53:08, within its hour. About 20 of its 48 minutes went to two waits on layer runs: the first was buffered output, the second the two runs the session thought were stuck from the start. The second wait came from the run's own tooling, a script with no per-step output, and not from the machine. It led straight to the wrong reading of those two layers (see summary). The recorded 0.8 CPU-hours is plausible: the four long processes alone add up to about 0.6 hours, and the session says it measured them from /proc. pmset and uptime do not exist on this Linux worker, as the summary says. No jobs are in flight. Disk and data size are well inside budget. The machine did not limit the science. The session's hour did, and so did the CPU cap in feed_capped.py, which is checked only between steps and so never stopped a run stuck inside one. Waiting are the overlap error at seed 1 (step to 5.90), the same-instant build, join and break loop at f* 0.4 (t 5.2528), the untraced hang at seed 2 (step after 6.24), and Chris's answer on the immovable-bounce rule.
discrepancies: Seed 2 at f* 0.3 and seed 1 at f* 0.4 are recorded as making no progress ('the first 0.01 step containing stack work did not finish'). Rerun with per-step output, the same code reaches 6.24 (27 stacks built) and 5.25 (19 built), past their old stall times of 5.823 and 4.910, before sticking in one step.
Seed 1 at f* 0.3 is recorded as reaching 5.88 with the error in the step to 5.89. Its own t_reached (5.89) shows it completed the step to 5.89 and failed in the step to 5.90.
Budget: the summary gives 562.2 CPU-hours spent this week. program check gives 290.5, and the same night's L0018 summary gave 293.6.
The line note gives about one second of Python per stack. The summary and evidence give 54.1 s over 28 stacks, about 1.9 s.
